meaning: He who is made of earth

phonemes.desc: Voiceless lateral affricate [tɬ], a single Nahuatl sound: 'tl' released with the tongue at the side teeth.
Long [aː], macron marking reconstructed vowel length.
[lok], final syllable; the name has been glossed as 'he who is made of earth' or 'he who is the embodiment of the earth'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'TLAH-lok' — start with the Nahuatl lateral affricate 'tl', hold the first 'a' long, and end with a firm 'ok'.

kin.label: Nahuatl
kin.form: Tlāloc, from tlālli ('earth') and a suffix suggesting quality or embodiment.

kin.label: Maya
kin.form: Chac, the hook-nosed rain god of the Classic Maya.

kin.label: Zapotec
kin.form: Cocijo, the lightning-rain deity of Monte Albán.

pronunciation.note: Tlāloc is Tier 1: the macron on ā preserves reconstructed Classical Nahuatl vowel length, and the initial tl- is a single distinctive phoneme impossible in English.

domains.title: Lord of Rain and Mountain
domains.subtitle: Water, Lightning, and Agricultural Life
domains.lead: Tlāloc is the ancient god of rain, lightning, and mountain water. His goggle eyes and jaguar fangs mark him as a being from before the Aztec empire, worshipped at Teotihuacan centuries before Tenochtitlan rose. Without his favour, maize withered and the Fifth Sun turned hostile.

cards.name: Tlalocan
cards.desc: His paradise for those who died by water, lightning, or water-borne disease.

cards.name: Mountain Dweller
cards.desc: He lives in caves and snow-capped peaks where clouds are born and rain is stored.

cards.name: Tlaloque
cards.desc: His multitude of assistants, the little rain gods who brew storms in mountain jars.

cards.name: Maize Lord
cards.desc: Rain is the precondition of corn; Tlāloc controls the timing of planting and harvest.

symbols.name: Goggle eyes
symbols.meaning: Attributes of the storm god across Mesoamerica, perhaps clouds or rain-filled sockets.

symbols.name: Jaguar fangs
symbols.meaning: The predatory power of thunder and the dangerous side of fertility.

symbols.name: Jade and blue paint
symbols.meaning: Signs of water, preciousness, and the verdant east.

symbols.name: Water-lily or frog
symbols.meaning: Creatures of standing water, omens of Tlāloc's presence.

mythology.lead: Tlāloc's myths turn on a single terrifying truth: the same rain that feeds can also drown, strike, or rot. He is generous and punitive in equal measure, and the Mexica state answered his moods with its most terrible gifts.

myths.title: The Abduction of Xōchiquetzal
myths.text: When the world was young, Xōchiquetzal — goddess of flowers, of weaving, and of love's delight — was the wife of Tlāloc. The account preserved in the Leyenda de los Soles tells how Tezcatlipoca, the lord of sorcery, desired her and abducted her to his own realm, and the tale spread widely enough to be retold in Ramírez de Fuenleal's Histoyre du Méchique. The marriage matters because it joins Tlāloc's water to the flowers — rain and blossom, the two halves of agricultural desire — and because its violence names a truth the farmers knew intimately. A god who can lose his bride to sorcery is a god whose gifts can be stolen too: the green world and the water world belong together, but nothing holds them together safely. The myth means that fertility is a marriage forever in danger of abduction.

myths.title: The Destruction of the Fourth Sun
myths.text: The Fourth Sun — the age called 4-Water — was the age of Tlāloc's consort Chalchiuhtlicue, Jade-Her-Skirt, and it ended as a water-god's age must: in a flood. The Leyenda de los Soles tells that the sky broke and rain fell for fifty-two years, until the people of that world were changed into fish and only a remnant survived as the seed of the Fifth Sun. The Histoyre du Méchique deepens the tragedy: Chalchiuhtlicue, falsely accused by her husband the sun of adultery, wept blood for fifty-two years, and the weeping drowned the world. The colonial sources disagree in their details, and modern scholars read the whole Sun-cycle as an Aztec theology of impermanence — every world, even a watery one, is born to end. The myth means that Tlāloc's element is never only the gentle rain of the milpa; it is the universal solvent, and the giver of maize keeps the memory of drowning.

myths.title: The Children of the Mountain
myths.text: The hardest evidence of Tlāloc's gravity is the child sacrifice the Mexica performed in his name. Sahagún's informants described the rites around the atezcalli, the 'house of water': children chosen for their beauty were carried in procession to the mountaintop shrines, and priests wearing Tlāloc's goggle-eyed regalia wept as they raised them up, so that the mountain rain-jars would pour. Durán adds the omen-reading that makes the rite almost unbearable: the children's tears on the road up foretold the season — abundant tears, abundant rain. Modern archaeology has found the theology in fact: in the offering caches of the Templo Mayor, excavated under Leonardo López Luján, the remains of children lie beside marine shells and greenstone. The rite means that in Aztec reciprocity there was no gift more precious than the newest life — and it is precisely this that makes Tlāloc impossible to domesticate as a mere 'rain spirit'.

myths.title: The Double Temple of Tenochtitlan
myths.text: At the center of Tenochtitlan rose the Templo Mayor, the double pyramid that married the city's two necessities. The south half, stained with red, belonged to Huitzilopochtli, god of war and the sun's ardor; the north half, washed in blue and hung with white paper streamers, belonged to Tlāloc, god of rain. Durán describes the blue-painted façade guarded by figures of the Tlaloque, and López Luján's excavations of the offering caches found the two halves speaking different languages: the war god's chambers held warriors and sacrificial flint; Tlāloc's held fish, crocodiles, coral, shells and jade — a drowned cosmos buried under the mountain. The pairing means that the Aztec state understood itself as an armed negotiation with water. War conquered enemies, tribute filled the treasury, but rain — Tlāloc's mood, read in the mountain caves — conquered everyone, kings included.

lore.syncretism: The goggle-eyed storm god appears across Mesoamerica under different names: Chac among the Maya, Cocijo among the Zapotec, and Dzahui among the Mixtec. Spanish missionaries equated Tlāloc with Saint John the Baptist and with water-related Christian figures, but the pre-contact cult proved tenacious. Even today, offerings of flowers and copal are left at mountain springs and caves in rural Mexico, often without conscious memory of the Aztec deity behind the practice.
lore.culturalLegacy: Tlāloc's most visible afterlife is the colossal monolith that guards the entrance of Mexico's National Museum of Anthropology. His image has also entered national iconography as a symbol of Mexico's indigenous past and its enduring relationship with water. In an era of drought and water scarcity, Tlāloc returns not as a remote antiquity but as a question: what have we forgotten about the sacred economy of rain?
lore.extendedMeditation:
Tlāloc is the god who holds back what we need most. Rain is not guaranteed; it is a negotiation conducted with ritual, sacrifice, and humility. In that sense Tlāloc is the most honest of agricultural deities: he does not promise abundance in exchange for virtue alone; he demands attention to the relationship between human need and natural limit.

To name him Tlāloc, with the long vowel and the impossible initial 'tl', is to remember that the rain is not ours. It belongs to the mountains, the caves, the clouds, and the ancient god whose goggle eyes watch the fields from every thunderhead.
lore.archaeology: The Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan, excavated from 1978 under Eduardo Matos Moctezuma and Leonardo López Luján, anchors Tlāloc's cult: his blue-painted half of the double pyramid and its offering caches of marine animals, coral, shells and greenstone. His worship is far older than the Aztec — goggle-eyed storm gods appear in the Tepantitla and Tlalocan murals of Teotihuacan (c. 450–650 CE) and in Classic-period Maya art as Chac. The colossal andesite monolith of Coatlinchan (Tlaloc's rain-mountain form, c. 13th–16th century), moved to Mexico City's National Museum of Anthropology in 1964, is among the largest pre-Columbian sculptures known; Mount Tlaloc's summit shrine above the Iztaccíhuatl still receives offerings.
lore.originalScriptNote: The etymology is debated. The most widely accepted reading derives Tlāloc from tlālli ('earth') plus a suffix meaning 'he who has the quality of' or 'he who is made of', giving 'he who is made of earth'—a striking name for a water deity, perhaps because rain rises from the earth and returns to it. Classical Nahuatl macrons mark vowel length; Spanish colonial orthography usually omits them. The final -c is the voiceless velar stop [k].
